newsitem.title: CANADA: Astronomers mull space fossils, lunar gamma rays.
newsitem.headline: Astronomers mull space fossils, lunar gamma rays.

text.p: About 1,300 astronomers gathered on Sunday to consider the mysteries of space such as black holes, intergalactic fossils and gamma rays supposedly emitted by the Moon.

The fine points of research into space are central to the five-day meeting of the American Astronomical Society in Toronto, but a spokesman for the group denied that recent reports of possible life on Mars and ice on the Moon do anything but spur public interest.

"There's almost no effect of those announcements on this meeting," AAS spokesman Steve Maran, who also works at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Centre outside Washington, said before the convention began.

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration touched off a world-wide scientific furore when it announced in August that it had found a meteorite in Antartica that appeared to originate from Mars and appeared to contain the fossilized remains of microscopic organisms.
And in December, the U.S. Defence Department reported that its instruments had indicated the presence of polar ice on the Moon, a significant finding because water is seen as a prerequisite for life.

While the bulk of the meeting will sidestep these reports, two lectures open to the public are geared to capitalise on the popularity of new discoveries about potential extraterrestrial life. One is on the search for past life on Mars and the other is a review of eight planets thought to be orbitting Sun-like stars outside our solar system.
Highlights of the five-day meeting are expected to include more confirmation of the existence of black holes, the matter- sucking theoretical features that have fascinated astronomers for decades.
In addition, among the 900 or so scientific papers presented will be:
-- research analysing what will happen to stars and galaxies -- and presumably planets like Earth -- when the universe ends;
-- a report that says the mysterious clouds associated with the Milky Way galaxy may in fact be interlopers from intergalactic space, possibly "fossils" of the raw material that formed the galaxy;
-- a new estimate of how old the universe is;

-- a fresh image showing the Moon giving off gamma rays; the notion that the Moon emits such radiation, long associated with nuclear bombs, is roughly as surprising to some astronomers as saying the Moon is made of green cheese, according to Maran.
The Moon's gamma rays are "obviously very weak or Neil Armstrong (the first astronaut to set foot on the Moon) would glow in the dark," Maran said in an interview.
William Shakespeare's "Hamlet" was also expected to make an appearance at the meeting in a lecture suggesting that characters in the play correspond to an astronomical framework.
Astronomers will also discuss the prospect of a new space- based telescope to be launched in the next several years, Maran said.
Another key function of the meeting is education about the nuts-and-bolts of earthly careers, he said.

"Frankly a great many of the younger astronomers and some of the others now just have to face up to that they're going to have to be really good teachers in order to have a prayer of having a job because the research jobs just aren't there any more," Maran said.
